title: Hold Up a Minute
body_text: There’s a situation over in J. Med. Chem. that has developed about a paper published there earlier this year, and after looking things over I can’t help but feel that someone involved - several people, actually - should end up feeling a bit embarrassed. See what you think! The featured paper in issue 12 back in June was Wang et al. of Jiangsu University on targeted protein degradation of dipeptidyl peptidase IV as a possible therapy for diabetes. Fine, DPP-IV inhibitors themselves are well-established therapeutic agents in that area, and when you have an inhibitor, one’s thoughts naturally turn to the possibility of a degrader, right? As a featured paper, there was an accompanying commentary that spoke about the significance of the work. The bifunctional molecule (which targets cereblon-mediated degradation) showed longer duration of action than plain pharmacological inhibition, although a disadvantage is that the molecule as it stands is not orally available. Fine, fine. Well, not so fine, actually. If you’ve actually worked with DPP-IV, then perhaps there is a nagging thought that is occurring to you about all this. It certainly seems to have occurred to Carlo Matera of Milan, who is the author of this Viewpoint article that has just come out in the journal. Matera points out that DPP-IV is an extracellular protein, and CRBN-mediated degradation is well established as in intracellular process. The original paper’s authors describe bifunctional that use the known inhibitor alogliptin as one end and a cereblon-binding imide as the other, but the alogliptin binding site is on the outside of the cell. By design, the alogliptin moiety of DeDPP4 should bind this pocket on the cell surface, keeping the CRBN ligand region in the extracellular space, which appears difficult to reconcile with the proposed mechanism since CRBN operates inside the cell as part of the ubiquitin-proteasome machinery. Even after endocytosis, the ectodomain should be exposed to the endosomal lumen rather than to the cytosolic CRBN. A CRBN-dependent proteasomal mechanism would therefore suggest the involvement of an additional noncanonical step that enables DPP-4-bound DeDPP4 to engage cytosolic CRBN. The nature of this step remains to be established. Malera goes on to detail a number of experiments that could be used to clarify this mismatch, and one has to imagine an unwritten coda of “. . .and which should have been in the original paper”. He notes, correctly, that degradation of cell-surface proteins is generally accomplished through lysosomal pathways, not proteasomal ones as demonstrated in the Wang et al. paper. That paper does mention that the DPP-IV protein seems to be internalized through endocytosis (a Lyso-Red assay), but that does not match up with the rest of their proposed mechanism at all, and the group seems to have not even looked at lysosomal degradation per se. You can’t help but think that someone should have raised such questions at the review stage, and the J. Med. Chem. editorial staff would be in a position to know if that happened. But if it did, why was this issue not addressed? As it stands, this is a very odd paper indeed, proposing degradation of a (very) extracellular protein through an intracellular mechanism in a way that i really don’t think has ever been described before. Discussion of that mechanism alone should have been a major focus of the publication - you’d think - but there is no mention of the groundbreaking strangeness of it at all, not that I can see. That also goes for the commentary article at the time, I should add. No one bats an eye. Well, an eye has now been batted, and I look forward to seeing what the resolution of all this turns out to be. Anyone want to make their predictions?
